objectives.title: A joined-up plan with our neighbours
objectives.summary: An integrated Bus Service Improvement Plan across Sussex
objectives.description:
Buses along this coast are planned by three separate authorities — West Sussex, Brighton & Hove and East Sussex — and the effect shows up in the timetable. Counting scheduled departures from the published timetable, Lancing has 65 bus stops averaging 32.8 departures each on a weekday. South Portslade, four miles along the same coast road but on the Brighton & Hove side of the boundary, has 43 stops averaging 116.8. That is roughly three and a half times the service per stop, for a comparable seaside neighbourhood on the same corridor.

Passengers do not experience a council boundary. They experience a bus that turns back, a ticket that stops being valid, and a timetable that thins out for no reason they can see.

The ask is that West Sussex works with Brighton & Hove City Council and East Sussex County Council on a genuinely integrated Bus Service Improvement Plan for the Sussex coast — one network planned end to end, with shared targets for frequency, hours and through-ticketing, rather than three plans that each stop at a line on a map.

objectives.title: More hours on the routes we already have
objectives.summary: Earlier mornings and later evenings on limited-frequency routes
objectives.description:
A bus route that does not run when people need to travel is not much use to them. Across Adur and Worthing a large number of routes carry only a handful of journeys a day, with nothing early enough for a shift starting at seven and nothing late enough to get home from an evening one. Care workers, hospital staff, hospitality workers and anyone doing a shift that does not fit office hours are left driving, paying for taxis, or not taking the job.

Adding journeys at each end of the day on routes that already exist is among the cheapest things that can be done for the network. The vehicles, the drivers' depots, the stops and the route registrations are all already in place; what is missing is an hour at the start and an hour or two at the end.

The ask is that West Sussex County Council works with the operators to identify the limited-frequency routes where an earlier first bus and a later last bus would open up shift work, and funds those journeys where they are not commercially viable on their own.

objectives.title: Express buses for commuters
objectives.summary: Faster peak-time links between Worthing and Brighton, and a second operator running them
objectives.description:
Getting between Worthing and Brighton at peak times is slow, and there is effectively only one company doing it. Both problems have the same fix.

Brighton & Hove Buses stop dead at Shoreham. Across the Adur and Worthing corridor they serve 576 stops, but not one in Lancing or Worthing. Their westernmost stop is Dacre Gardens, and the 28 stops they reach beyond Shoreham are all on routes 2, 2B, 59 and 59A running north up the Adur valley towards Steyning and Upper Beeding — not west along the coast.

West of Shoreham there are 736 stops with a bus service. Compass reaches 395 of them and Stagecoach 386. Brighton & Hove reaches 28, all of them in the valley. So Lancing and Worthing sit on the edge of Brighton's network and are served by everyone except the operator whose network they most need to reach. A Worthing passenger has no Brighton & Hove option at all, and no competitive alternative on the corridor.

Brighton & Hove served Lancing and Worthing within living memory. Bringing those services back west would give the coast a second operator, a real choice of bus, and a direct link into the Brighton network that today needs a change and a second ticket.

There is also a cheap way to make the existing service faster: split a frequent route so that at peak times every other journey runs express, calling only at the main stops. That needs no extra vehicles and no extra drivers — it is a timetable change — and it would cut the journey time for people travelling the full length of the corridor.

objectives.title: Merge the Stagecoach DayRider zones
objectives.summary: One coastal DayRider covering Worthing and Brighton, at the £6 each already costs
objectives.description:
Stagecoach sells a Worthing DayRider and a Brighton DayRider at £6 each, and the two zones do not overlap anywhere. Of the stops Stagecoach serves, 361 sit in the Worthing zone and 186 in the Brighton zone, and not a single one sits in both. Every journey along the coast between the two towns therefore crosses a boundary.

That leaves two options, and both are bad. Buy both tickets, at £12. Or buy a Gold DayRider at £8.50 — a ticket valid across Hampshire, Surrey and Berkshire, bought purely to travel from Worthing to Brighton and back.

For someone commuting five days a week, the Gold ticket costs about £12.50 a week more than a single zone ticket would if one covered the trip — roughly £575 a year, paid by people making one of the most ordinary journeys in the area.

The ask is simple, and it costs the operator nothing in new mileage: one coastal DayRider covering both zones, priced at the same £6 the two separate tickets already cost.

objectives.title: One ticket for the whole coast
objectives.summary: Mutual ticket acceptance between operators, at day-ticket prices
objectives.description:
At 502 of the 1,633 stops in the Adur, Worthing and Brighton corridor — almost a third of them — more than one company's buses call. At those stops, the bus that happens to arrive first decides whether the ticket in your pocket is valid. A Stagecoach DayRider is not accepted on a Brighton & Hove or Metrobus service, so passengers either watch a bus go past and wait for the right livery, or pay twice for the same journey.

This is not an impossible ask, because it already half exists. Metrovoyager is valid on Brighton & Hove services, and networkSAVER is valid on Metrobus within its zone. The gap is Stagecoach, which accepts nobody and is accepted by nobody. The all-operator South Downs Discovery Ticket does exist at £10, but it is priced and marketed as a day-out rover rather than a commuter fare, and it is not valid on the N700 or the N1.

The ask is mutual ticket acceptance across the corridor at ordinary day-ticket prices, so that a ticket bought for a journey is valid on whichever bus actually makes that journey.

objectives.title: Night service that goes west
objectives.summary: Affordable late-night travel westward from Brighton, beyond the N700
objectives.description:
After the last daytime buses, travel westward out of Brighton depends almost entirely on one route, the N700. It runs along a narrow coastal corridor, it is expensive, and it is not covered by the ordinary day tickets most passengers already hold.

The practical effect is that an evening in Brighton ends early for anyone living in Adur or Worthing, or ends in a taxi fare that costs more than the evening did. That falls hardest on the people least able to absorb it: hospitality and night-shift staff travelling home from work, and younger passengers without a car.

The ask is more night service running west from Brighton into Adur and Worthing, at fares consistent with the daytime network rather than at a premium — and, at minimum, for existing day tickets and passes to be honoured on the night services that already run.

objectives.title: Accessible buses and stops for everyone
objectives.summary: Audio-visual next-stop information on every bus
objectives.description:
Every bus should announce and display the route, the direction of travel and the next stop. Without it, a passenger who cannot see the street or cannot hear the driver has no reliable way of knowing where they are, and the practical result is that people stop travelling independently.

This is not simply a request — it is the law, and the deadline has almost run out. The Public Service Vehicles (Accessible Information) Regulations 2023 (SI 2023/715) require audible and visible route, direction and next-stop information on local bus services, phased by vehicle age: vehicles first used from 1 October 2019 had to comply by 1 October 2024; those first used between October 2014 and September 2019 by 1 October 2025; and the rest of the fleet, anything first used before 30 September 2014, by 1 October 2026.

The ask is that operators confirm publicly which of their vehicles serving Adur and Worthing are compliant and which are not, with a date for the rest; and that the councils, as the bodies funding supported services and letting contracts, make compliance a condition of that funding.

objectives.title: Clear, real-time information everywhere
objectives.summary: E-Ink live displays at every stop and one real-time app across operators
objectives.description:
Most bus stops in Adur and Worthing still carry only a paper timetable. If the bus is late, cancelled or diverted, there is no way to find that out while standing at the stop, and a passenger without a smartphone has no way of finding it out at all. Waiting twenty minutes for a bus that is never coming is one of the things that persuades people never to try the bus again.

Two things would fix most of it. First, E-Ink live departure displays at as many stops as possible: they are far cheaper to install and run than traditional powered signs, need no mains connection, are readable in daylight, and are already in use elsewhere in West Sussex. Second, real-time data published openly and completely by every operator, so that any app — including the councils' own — can show the whole network rather than one company's part of it, with fares and disruption information included.

The ask is a costed programme for live displays at the busiest stops, prioritising interchanges and stops serving hospitals, schools and employment sites; and a requirement that operators publish complete, accurate real-time and fares data for the whole corridor.
